title: Urban economic concentration can coexist with rising poverty when housing, services, finance, and climate resilience fail to scale
source_unit: World Bank, Madagascar Urbanization Review: Leveraging Cities as Drivers of Growth and Structural Transformation
geography: Madagascar, with national, capital-city, secondary-city, and urban-service comparisons

observations.period: 2026 review; urban economic concentration and poverty

denominator.unit: Madagascar urban economy and population frame

urban_gdp_share.unit: percent of national GDP attributed to cities

capital_gdp_share.unit: percent of national GDP attributed to Antananarivo

secondary_city_poverty_change.value: poverty in secondary cities increased from 46 percent to 61 percent over the past decade
secondary_city_poverty_change.unit: reported change in urban poverty share

growth_poverty_gap.value: urban economic weight is not translating into effective poverty reduction or inclusive growth

observations.method: World Bank country urbanization review using urban economic, poverty, infrastructure, service, fiscal, and climate-risk analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary reports national and city-level aggregates and does not identify individual household trajectories, causal effects of particular urban policies, or the full timing of the poverty increase.
observations.subgroup: Urban residents, especially people in secondary cities, low-income households, informal workers, and residents of underserved settlements.
observations.counterinterpretation: Urban concentration can still create a platform for productivity and poverty reduction if land, services, fiscal authority, and investment are coordinated; the observed gap is not proof that urbanization itself causes poverty.

observations.period: 2026 review; urban housing, services, and hazard exposure

denominator.unit: percent of urban residents in Madagascar

informal_unplanned_settlements.unit: percent or more of urban citizens living in informal and unplanned settlements

direct_drinking_water_medium_small_citie.unit: percent or less of residents in medium and small cities with direct drinking-water supply

waste_drainage.value: more than half of solid waste generated in cities is dumped in drainage canals

risk.value: informal and underserved settlements are often located in hazard-prone and high-risk areas, amplifying flood and public-health exposure

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of urban settlement, water, sanitation, waste, drainage, and hazard conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The summary uses threshold and directional statistics rather than a complete city-by-city service dataset; access, quality, reliability, and household coping are not interchangeable.
observations.subgroup: Residents of informal settlements, households without direct water access, people exposed to flooding, and communities relying on informal service arrangements.
observations.counterinterpretation: Service deficits can be reduced through upgrading, land administration, municipal coordination, and targeted investment; informal settlement does not imply identical conditions across neighborhoods.

hazards.value: floods, cyclones, sea-level rise, and coastal erosion affect Malagasy cities

disaster_event_change.unit: fold increase in disaster-related events impacting Madagascar over the last 20 years

development_reversal.value: recurring climate-driven disasters can produce economic and physical losses and reverse development gains

observations.method: World Bank urban climate-risk and disaster-resilience synthesis linked to housing, infrastructure, and development conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The reported event multiplier does not estimate city-specific damage, household recovery, attribution of every event to climate change, or the effect of a particular resilience investment.
observations.subgroup: Urban poor households, residents in hazard-prone settlements, coastal communities, municipal responders, and service users dependent on fragile infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Risk-informed land use, drainage, resilient infrastructure, early warning, and social protection can reduce realized losses even where hazard exposure continues to rise.

observations.period: 2026 review; city finance and implementation capacity

denominator.unit: percent of city revenue and budget in the World Bank fiscal-capacity summary

central_transfers.unit: percent or less of city revenues coming from central-government fiscal transfers

capital_investment.unit: percent or less of city budgets spent on capital investment

capacity_route.value: weak mandates, limited fiscal resources, low own-source revenue, and weak data systems constrain municipal service delivery and resilient urban investment

proposed_response.value: the review proposes integrated national-regional-municipal policy, coordinated land and service reform, resilient infrastructure finance, and stronger city institutions and data

observations.method: World Bank institutional and municipal-finance assessment with a four-pillar urbanization roadmap.
observations.uncertainty: The recommendations are a policy roadmap, not an evaluation of implementation or proof that any one financing or decentralization reform will improve household outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Municipal governments, residents dependent on public services, taxpayers, informal-settlement communities, and national agencies responsible for urban policy and transfers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Central coordination can sometimes produce scale and equalization; greater municipal autonomy without reliable revenue, skills, accountability, and data could reproduce uneven capacity.

related_sources.claim: World Bank report PDF linked from the official publication page; the document server was not directly retrievable during acquisition.
World Bank urban development context for cities, services, resilience, and inclusive growth.

boundary: This record adds a named-country urban realization layer to the broader urban housing and infrastructure theme. It is a World Bank country review and public summary, not respondent-level data, a longitudinal household panel, a city-by-city causal evaluation, or proof that a proposed reform has been implemented.

The linked report PDF was retained as a related source but was not claimed as directly retrieved.
